speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: asked the Minister for Education whether the Ministry will consider having all GCE examination papers to be prepared and marked locally to minimise the risk associated with having the papers shipped and marked overseas.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: asked the Minister for Education with regard to GCE "N", "O" and "A" Levels examinations (a) whether examination scripts of all subjects will be scanned, digitalised and marked onscreen by the end of 2019 or will some subjects be exempted; (b) whether any overseas examination boards have conducted e-exams for examinations of similar level; (c) whether the Ministry has conducted trials or is conducting trials for holding e-exams for some subjects; and (d) whether schools and students are currently equipped to conduct and complete examinations digitally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I also note that Mr Murali Pillai1 has filed a similar question on this issue for the next Sitting, so I hope my answer today will also address the Member's question.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOE and the Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board (SEAB) decide on the standards and the award of grades for our national examinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the same time, we engage Cambridge Assessment to develop and mark our GCE "N", "O", "A" Level examinations because they have strong global expertise and experience in these areas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This arrangement has worked well for many years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Cambridge Assessment in turn taps on about 2,200 professors and experienced educators from universities and higher institutions to mark the scripts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, if we were to mark all the scripts locally, it requires a very substantial amount of highly qualified resources.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As these are required during the school vacation period, we need to be mindful too about the workload and well-being of our teachers if all subjects are to be marked locally, and also the tight timeline between the examinations and the release of results.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the years, Cambridge Assessment has also taken their role very professionally and seriously.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, following the recent "O" Level Additional Mathematics incident, Cambridge Assessment has reinforced the instructions given to their examiners on the handling and movement of scripts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Examiner concerned will also not be engaged to mark scripts in future; it cannot be helped.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Overall, this collaboration between MOE and Cambridge Assessment continues to be useful and necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next question then is whether we can improve the situation by marking the scripts electronically, to ensure the safety and integrity of the scripts, and prevent future losses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, since 2015 and before the recent incidents, SEAB and Cambridge Assessment have been working closely on a planned move to transit the distribution and marking of hardcopy GCE Level answer scripts to on-screen marking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are many professional advantages: tabulation of scores become much faster and efficient; there is no need to handle voluminous physical scripts; we can readily generate data to study how students perform in various papers, sections, or even questions, which will help us improve instructions and teaching.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given the large number of answer scripts, the implementation of on-screen marking was carried out in phases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 2017, we implemented this for GCE "N" Level examinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 2018 last year, this was extended to some GCE "O" Level examinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: By the end of this year, we are on track to mark on-screen almost all of GCE Level written scripts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From 2020, locally developed examination papers, namely GCE Normal (Technical) Level Basic Mother Tongue Language and "O" Level Literature in Mother Tongue Language, will be marked on-screen and more local papers will be included over the subsequent few years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are some examination papers that are not suitable for on-screen marking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, Science Practical examination scripts cannot be marked on-screen as these answer scripts may be contaminated with chemicals which makes them unsuitable for scanning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Other examinations like drama or art are obviously also not suitable for on-screen marking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Members have also asked if we could go beyond on-screen marking to conduct electronic-examinations, on-screen examinations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are a few examination boards that have implemented e-examinations, for example, the SAT test by US College Board for college admission.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The approach in Singapore is to use e-examinations when there is clear benefit over paper-based tests.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, SEAB has already implemented e-oral exams across all levels for Mother Tongue Language subjects.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We use video clips to set the context, and that enables a richer and more meaningful interaction compared to just showing a picture, which was what we went through, probably.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will be extended to the GCE "N" Level English in 2019 and "O" Level English in 2020.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have introduced computer-based writing examination as a pilot in a few subjects, such as the GCE "O" and "A" Level Mother Tongue Language Syllabus B's Paper 1 and GCE "A" Level H2 Mother Tongue Language and Literature.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So far the feedback has been positive as the candidates found the e-examination more engaging and authentic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is possible that in time to come, more written examinations can be administered on screen as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Students can more readily cut and paste, edit their essays, move paragraphs around.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They can be asked to respond to an email, write a blog or a social media post, all these better reflect real life situations that students will go through later in life.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we are still some time away from that future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to take into account the readiness of schools and students.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More importantly, notwithstanding the high computer penetration rate amongst our population, we should not inadvertently disadvantage students who may not be exposed to computers as much as others.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ideally, e-examinations needs to be aligned to the schools’ use of technology in teaching and learning.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we move towards more of e-examinations and online marking, I think that will take several years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will we consider doing entirely all of our GCE marking locally?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Minister mentioned that, yes, it will require a lot more markers and teachers, but I think we do have the capability here and would it not be easier to fly in some of the markers and auditors from Cambridge to audit the marking, rather than leaving our papers overseas where our exam papers have been taken onboard trains and that is why they were lost.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because when we do marking here, even for the PSLE papers, papers are not removed from the marking centres at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, while you may save time transporting the scripts, the amount of extra resources required is huge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And I am quite mindful of the workload of teachers especially during vacation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to turnaround this in a very short time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, on balance, the collaboration with Cambridge Assessment has been working well, not withstanding this couple of incidents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Even as we move to e-marking, this is a collaboration that, on the whole, logistically, taking into account the resources and costs required, it is still worthwhile for us to do so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Pending any future changes to the marking method and the examination method, since the last incident, have any new measures been taken to improve the transportation and delivery of the scripts to UK and back to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The protocol is all there, that once a marker has scripts in their hands, they are not supposed to leave it behind, and I think this is what happened in this particular incident.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They have since tightened the instructions, conveyed to all the markers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The marker who was involved, he would not be engaged anymore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think with their efforts and constant reminders, we can mitigate such risks to the minimum extend possible.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Maybe not quite directly related to these current questions that you are managing right now.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Just looking at the potential risks of such summative assessment formats such as the GCE exams, would we consider, going forward, to minimise the dependence on such summative assessment formats and look at more at how we can balance such summative exams with students' portfolios for instance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Because for the students whose exams papers are missing, they get a certain prorated grade which they feel that sometimes it is fair, sometimes it is not quite fair.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: But if they have a student portfolio, they know that it is their work, built up over time, that they can depend on for admission to the next entry level in their education journey.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a question about summative versus formative assessment.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we have more formative assessments, more regular tests, there is actually more risks of losing scripts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, I think it is a valid question on the direction that education is going.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given our system today, summative assessments will still play a big role.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because parents and students depend a lot on PSLE for allocation of places in Secondary schools, and from Secondary schools moving to JC or Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, I think what we ought to refine is at the admission level.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That beyond looking at the summative test result, can we look at portfolio, as the Member mentioned, performances in other areas outside of academic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, DSA scheme, EAE schemes that we had introduced and refined over the years, all these will help towards the move away from over-relying on summative tests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the Autonomous Universities, we have to complete all our marking locally within a very short span of time as well and it is a very stressful period for all of the Faculty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But I wonder if the Ministry could commit, for example, to studying this issue of the costs of arranging for all of the marking locally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What would be the cost implications of doing that versus the current arrangement with Cambridge Assessment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The reason why I asked this is, I think there should be no questions internationally about the credibility of our examination system if it were to be done all locally.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think Singapore has established a good reputation in that regard and I am confident that if we were to do it locally, we should have no issues with the reputation of students' credentials.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the whole concern about transport of scripts which really underpins this concern, will not arise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I fully agree with the Member that Singapore has a good reputation in education, there is high regard internationally for our education system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are in a good position to do this ourselves and harness the resources to mark the papers, set the questions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But I think we are where we are too because of a certain earnestness to learn from different systems around the world and to work with different credible, reputable systems around the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And this approach led us to working with Cambridge.
